messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Carlos Carlos, a 54-year-old Latin American parole officer, has been haunted by his experience of police violence for over two years. The traumatic event occurred during what was meant to be a routine traffic stop. Carlos had pulled over a suspected drug dealer when he was suddenly confronted by several officers in full riot gear. They accused him of misconduct and violently arrested him without any provocation. This event left Carlos feeling violated and betrayed, an experience that has since shaped his daily life. The memory of the incident is fragmented and incomplete. Whenever Carlos tries to recall it, he finds himself pushing the details away before they can fully surface, leaving gaps in his recollection. The moments that do emerge feel surreal, making him question whether it really happened to him. This lack of clarity adds to his distress, as he struggles with a sense of disbelief and confusion. Carlos's work as a parole officer has become increasingly difficult due to the trauma. On the job, even small triggers like people misbehaving or his own heart racing can send him into a state of heightened alertness. The unusual silence in courtrooms or during interviews makes him feel that something dangerous is about to happen, and he constantly scans his surroundings for any signs of danger. These reactions are not just fleeting; they have become a persistent part of his daily routine. What frightens Carlos most is the feeling of betrayal by those he trusted. He was certain that the police officers who attacked him were supposed to uphold justice, yet they violated that trust in an act that felt deeply unfair and unjustified. This sense of betrayal has only deepened as time has passed, given that no action has been taken against those responsible for his treatment. The injustice he experienced has also led Carlos to feel like the institutions meant to protect him have failed him completely. He is acutely aware that the memory of this event remains incomplete and unreal, reinforcing his negative appraisals. His constant fear that something dangerous will happen in moments of silence or sudden movements exacerbates these feelings, creating a cycle where each trigger reinforces both his threat perception and his sense of betrayal. Carlos’s daily life has become an intricate dance around these triggers. At work, he avoids situations that might remind him of the event, such as certain neighborhoods or types of cases. This avoidance has strained his relationships with colleagues who do not understand his sudden withdrawal from tasks he once handled with ease. His marriage is also affected; his wife finds it difficult to comprehend why he seems so anxious and on edge all the time. The accumulation of these experiences over time has made Carlos feel increasingly isolated and overwhelmed. He finally sought help when a minor incident at work—a loud noise—sent him into such an intense state of anxiety that he felt unable to continue his job effectively without support. What he hopes for is a sense of normalcy and the ability to trust again, both in himself and in the institutions he once believed in. Carlos’s current state is one of deep turmoil, where each trigger reinforces his threat perception and negative appraisals, making it increasingly difficult for him to function normally. He needs help to break this cycle and regain a sense of safety and justice in his life.
